VERA: Scaling Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution

Abstract

Competent agents need precise and verifiable environments, such as sandboxes that are resumable at any stage and evolve from observable evidence. However, most long-horizon work exposes how rare these are: for example, an agent in medical research must ground a finding, classify it, and write a report over dozens of dependent steps, yet recent environments score only the outcome. To address the challenges in stable training, we present VERA, which builds such environments at scale and lets agents evolve on them. VERA builds these environments from initial trajectories: an agent writes rubrics, executable checks, a judge verifies each sandbox, and only those that pass enter the training bank. On these environments, VERA alternates between two updates: train the model with rubric rewards, or edit the harness skills. We also create a verifier which gates model checkpoints and harness edits using explicit development-set acceptance criteria. This attribution distinguishes VERA’s co-evolution from single-axis baselines: its updates target not only the cause but the outcome. With an open-source corpus of 9,000+ long-horizon verifiable environments, a 9B model paired with its co-evolved agent beats the strongest baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 points in the two domains. At 27B, it surpasses the baseline on AutoCoWorkBench (71.6) and AutoMedBench (80.7), transfers to unseen workflows, and retains general capabilities.

1 Introduction

One ultimate ambition of agentic artificial intelligence is a system that improves from its own attempts and grows into an expert-level generalist. AI has taken visible steps toward this ambition in software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026), computer-use, office automation (Yao et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024). Yet the ambition remains unrealized for the long-horizon research. Consider medical research: a competent research agent must ground findings in an image, classify them, and compose a report under expert scrutiny, a workflow of dozens of dependent steps in which one early mistake invalidates the entire workflow. Unlike coding and office workflows, where we can find trajectory resources online, very few AI systems today can learn to master research workflows because they lack practical environments. We argue that the bottleneck is not the learning algorithm but the environment.

In modern agent training, an environment contains a reusable sandbox, a task packaged with its tools, workspace, and initial state, together with a mechanism that scores success from observable evidence. Reinforcement Learning (RL) consumes such environments, and self-improvement is impossible without them. Current practice builds environments in two ways, and both break down on long-horizon agentic work. First, manual construction pipelines (Pan et al., 2024; Jain et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) synthesize executable tasks and define success by a test suite. Agents improve themselves through test signals, through RL with verifiable rewards (Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025), on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024), or reflection training (Bi et al., 2026); or through the harness, skills, tools, and execution rules, via verbal reflection (Shinn et al., 2023), skill libraries (Wang et al., 2023), prompt and workflow search (Khattab et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), and harness-code evolution (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Lee et al., 2026). Recent systems co-evolve both (Wu et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026a), but without verified evidence of a failure, each change is judged only by scores or pass rates. Second, evaluation benchmarks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; Chan et al., 2024; Schmidgall and others, 2024; Zuo et al., 2025) are also environments that are curated by hand and score only the outcome. This process does not measure rewards or localize failures in the intermediate stages. The result is a structural gap: environments yield no stage-level verified evidence, and self-evolution loops cannot gain from precision failures. In words, no precise verifiable environments.

In this paper, we present VERA (Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution), which closes this gap by constructing open verifiable environments and letting the agent evolve on them. Our starting observation is that benchmark trajectories already contain everything a verifiable environment starts with: initial states, tool interactions, and their observable effects. A data pipeline, Auto-Rubric, converts such trajectories into training sandboxes. A coding agent writes binary rubrics over action arguments, execution effects, artifacts, and outputs; stage-wise sandboxes restore the workspace at the start of each stage: plan, setup, verify, execute, submit, so a long workflow decomposes into verifiable units, while end-to-end sandboxes use an LLM for tool calls (Zhang et al., 2026). Executable code checks and an agent judge inspect the workspace, and a failed executable check overrides any judge score. On these environments, the VERA loop evolves the agent in alternating rounds: LLM Attribution reads stage-wise rubric scores and execution traces to decide which step is failing; model rounds run full-parameter GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with rubric rewards that a Reward Verifier checks against rollout evidence; harness rounds add, merge, or remove skills, accepted only when paired reruns with the frozen model confirm improvement. This design solves three problems: rewards come from what the agent actually did rather than from tests, long tasks are scored step by step, and only one part of the agent changes at a time, so every gain has clear evidence.

We evaluate VERA in two complementary domains: Medical Research and Automation. AutoMedBench (Liu et al., 2026b) and AutoCoWorkBench cover practical work and specialized research workflows, respectively; both evaluate complete long-horizon tasks with process and outcome scores, allowing us to assess execution quality alongside task success. At 9B, co-evolution outperforms the strongest single-axis baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 Overall points, respectively, with ablations confirming the importance of updating both the model and its harness. At 27B, VERA reaches 71.6 on AutoCoWorkBench and 80.7 on AutoMedBench, surpassing Claude Opus 4.8 on the former and coming within 1.2 points on the latter. It also transfers to unseen workflows on Automation-Bench (Zapier, 2026) and AgentClinic (Schmidgall and others, 2024). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B backbones, domain performance increases across the tested backbones; only at 27B are general capabilities also retained and mostly improved, suggesting that stronger backbones better support self-evolution without sacrificing broader capabilities.

To the best of our knowledge, we build the first large-scale verifiable environments for the joint self-evolution of an LLM and its harness, and we open-source the resulting 9,000+ environment corpus. To summarize, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    VERA: verifiable environment scaling for recursive self-improvement. We turn benchmark trajectories into restartable, rubric-scored sandboxes for long-horizon agent tasks, with an admission loop that accepts only environments executable and scoreable from observable evidence.

  • •

    Co-evolution of the LLM and its harness on VERA environments. Rubrics provide verified evidence; LLM Attribution turns it into model and harness reports; the two components update in alternating rounds, and verifiers decide whether each update is kept.

  • •

    An open resource of 9,000+ verifiable long-horizon training environments and scaling to a 27B backbone. At 9B the co-evolved agent exceeds the strongest single-axis baseline by 10.3 (CoWork) and 13.0 (MedResearch) Overall points; at 27B it surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 on AutoCoWorkBench and comes within 1.2 points on AutoMedBench.

2 Method

We introduce VERA (Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution). Its goal is to let a long-horizon agent improve itself from its own attempts, without human labels, through rule-guided self-evolution: verified rubrics provide the evidence, LLM Attribution turns the evidence into model-side and harness-side reports, and verifiers decide whether each update is kept. Concretely, VERA consists of two pipelines (Figure 1): a data pipeline, Auto-Rubric, which turns benchmark trajectories into verified, restartable training environments (Figure 3); and a training pipeline that co-evolves the LLM and its harness on these environments in alternating rounds. The rest of this section presents each pipeline in turn.

2.1 VERA: Co-Evolution Method

The VERA loop improves two parts of the agent in alternating rounds: the LLM and the harness (its skills, tools, and execution rules).

Model training freezes the harness; harness testing freezes the model; rubrics and verifiers stay fixed within a round. Any gain is therefore attributable to a single axis, which is what lets rubric evidence decide what to change next. To choose that axis, each round starts by evaluating the current pair on development tasks. LLM Attribution reads the stage-wise scores and execution traces and produces two reports: an LLM Report that locates the target stage, the stage with the most frequent model-attributed failures, and a Harness Report that lists missing or misleading procedures. Rubrics provide the evidence; verifiers decide acceptance. Infrastructure failures are excluded. Appendix G illustrates how the two reports direct model as well as skill updates in a CoWork example.

Update the model, freeze the harness.

The model makes new attempts in the stage-wise and end-to-end sandboxes, and full-parameter GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) updates its weights with rubric scores as rewards, following the execution/training separation of Agent Lightning (Luo et al., 2025). The optimizer and budget match our GRPO baseline; only the learning signal differs: rewards come from stage rubrics, and the curriculum follows the target stage. For stage kk, let zk,j∈{0,1}z_{k,j}\in\{0,1\} be the score of rubric item jj, wk,j>0w_{k,j}>0 its weight, and hk∈{0,1}h_{k}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether all mandatory checks pass:

rk=hk​∑jwk,j​zk,j∑jwk,j,Re2e=g⁡[λ​p+(1−λ)​c],r_{k}=h_{k}\frac{\sum_{j}w_{k,j}z_{k,j}}{\sum_{j}w_{k,j}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{e2e}}=g\,[\lambda p+(1-\lambda)c], (1)

where pp is a process score, c∈{0,1}c\in\{0,1\} a verified completion signal, g∈{0,1}g\in\{0,1\} a trajectory-level hard gate, and λ\lambda the process weight. CoWork sets pp to the mean of the five stage rewards, with λ=0.2\lambda{=}0.2 and g=1g{=}1; MedResearch sets pp to a judged process score, with λ=0.5\lambda{=}0.5 and g=0g{=}0 upon verified reward hacking or a hard-gate failure (Appendix E). In words: a stage earns the weighted fraction of rubric items it passes, and nothing if a mandatory check fails; the end-to-end reward gives credit for partial progress but stays responsible for verified completion. Before a reward enters training, the Reward Verifier checks the rollout evidence behind it. Training focuses on the target stage from the LLM Report; neighboring stages and complete tasks stay in the mix, so stage-level gains must survive the full workflow. A candidate checkpoint that fails acceptance falls back to the previously accepted checkpoint. Unlike harness edits, model updates need not yield an immediate improvement. A candidate checkpoint is accepted if its development-benchmark score decreases by no more than 20% relative to the previously accepted checkpoint.

Update the harness, freeze the model.

The Harness Report turns failed rubric items into candidate skill edits: add a missing skill, merge overlapping ones, or remove a harmful one (e.g., adding early_stop or merging stage_tracker and plan_tracker in Figure 1). The same LLM performs attribution and writes the proposed skill edits. Harness updates are restricted to skills; tools and execution rules remain fixed. The Harness Verifier tests each edit with paired runs on the development set: the same frozen model on the same tasks, with and without the edit, so only the edit can cause the difference. An edit is accepted only if it improves its target stage, causes no end-to-end regression, and passes safety checks; otherwise the current harness is kept. At most three edits are accepted per round. In addition, an edit must pass self-tests and improve the Overall development score by at least 5 %\% points. How often a skill is used is not evidence that it helps; only the paired comparison counts. Across rounds, the two axes feed each other: accepted skills change the next round’s training distribution, and the improved model exposes the next harness weakness. Appendix I provides concrete skill proposals and verifier decisions.

2.2 Auto-Rubric

Rubrics

A coding agent reads the task statement, the tool documentation, the execution logs, and the workspace, then writes a rubric: a list of binary checks, each scored in {0,1}\{0,1\}, over action arguments, execution effects, artifacts, and output quality. Every check must be verifiable from observable evidence, so a rubric is at once the completion condition of a task and the evidence required to prove it.

Sandboxes

As shown in Figure 3, we construct CoWork sandboxes from Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026), SWE-Bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), MLE-Bench (Chan et al., 2024), and medical sandboxes from AutoMedBench (Liu et al., 2026b) and MedXpertQA (Zuo et al., 2025) workflows. Inspired by BaT’s staged medical training (Liu et al., 2026a), we adopt five stages—plan, setup, verify, execute, and submit—to explore transfer across domains. A coding agent restores each stage’s starting workspace, retains its query and interaction history, and attaches domain- and stage-specific rubrics grounded in task requirements and artifacts (Appendix C). Each stage can then be practiced and scored independently. End-to-end sandboxes retain the full workflow while an LLM surrogate simulates time-consuming tool calls (Ren et al., 2025). Both types undergo executable checks and Agent Judge verification before entering the training bank.

Verification

Every candidate sandbox passes two kinds of checks. Executable code checks cover tool and skill schemas, restored states, and deterministic outputs. The Agent Judge, going beyond LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023a), interacts with the workspace and checks arguments, execution effects, artifacts, and output context. A failed executable check or official verifier overrides any judge score. Sandboxes that fail are revised or rejected; only environments that run and score from evidence enter the training bank. This admission loop is what makes the corpus, and later the rewards, resistant to reward hacking. Appendix H illustrates verifier decisions; Appendix D shows the resulting SFT records, RL starting states, and curation checks.

3 Experimental Setup

We evaluate whether verified model–harness co-evolution improves long-horizon agents in CoWork and MedResearch. Our experiments compare learning methods, isolate each update axis, and assess scaling, transfer, and general-capability retention. Domains and benchmarks. Each domain uses separate agents and training sandboxes, with evaluation instances excluded from training. CoWork evaluation uses AutoCoWorkBench and SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024); MedResearch uses the current seven-track AutoMedBench-Lite release (Liu et al., 2026b; AutoMedBench Contributors, 2026) (denoted AutoMedBench throughout) and MedXpertQA Text (Zuo et al., 2025). Automation-Bench (public 600, v1.0.6) (Zapier, 2026) and AgentClinic (Schmidgall and others, 2024) assess transfer. Appendix A describes the benchmark task organization and scoring units; Appendix B lists the evaluation protocols and harness settings. Comparisons and scaling. At 9B, we compare prompting, harness optimization, model training, and joint evolution under shared training data and matched fixed-harness RL budgets (Appendix F). Harness-only and LLM-only variants at 9B and 27B isolate each component. We evaluate full co-evolution at 4B, 9B, and 27B, compare 27B agents with frontier models, and measure capability retention on AIME 2026 (Mathematical Association of America, 2026), ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), GPQA-Diamond (Rein and others, 2023), and IF-Bench (Pyatkin and others, 2025). Implementation details. We use Qwen3.5 at 4B and 9B (Qwen Team, 2026a; Qwen Team, 2026b) and Qwen3.8 at 27B (Qwen Team, 2026c). Each run starts with SFT, followed by alternating model and harness updates. Training settings and execution configurations appear in Appendices E and B.

4 Results

4.1 VERA Agentic Co-Evolution Outperforms Single-Axis Optimization

VERA improves agent performance across both domains by jointly evolving the model and its harness (Table 2). It outperforms harness evolving with ADAS (Hu et al., 2025), LLM evolving training including GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and RaR (Gunjal et al., 2025), and harness and llm joint evolution with COS-PLAY (Wu et al., 2026b). On AutoCoWorkBench, VERA-Code Agent reaches 31.0 Overall, exceeding the strongest single-axis baseline, ADAS (20.7), by 10.3 points. On AutoMedBench (Liu et al., 2026b), VERA-Med Agent reaches 69.1, exceeding its harness-only variant (56.1) by 13.0 points. The full method also leads on SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and MedXpertQA Text (Zuo et al., 2025), with 54.2 and 50.8 Pass@1, respectively. These suites use official scoring protocols that differ from the training rubrics. Together, these results support the effectiveness of verified co-evolution across both stage-scored workflows and final-task evaluations.

Robustness

The same loop drives both lines and improves both: one method, two tool ecosystems, no cross-domain interference, see Table 2. The robustness comes from the environments themselves, the same verifiable, restartable sandboxes feed the loop in both domains. The lines improve along different axes, harness and model contribute roughly equally on CoWork, while the harness arm carries more of the Med gain, so a full assessment needs the axis-level ablation and the scale analysis below.

Ablation Study.

Freezing one axis costs about half the gain, see Table 2. On AutoMedBench, LLM-only reaches 43.3 and harness-only 56.1, against 69.1 for the full loop; on AutoCoWorkBench, 18.9 and 18.2 against 31.0.

4.2 VERA Scales to 27B and Reaches Frontier-Level Performance

Figure 2 compares complete agents with productivity harnesses, where VERA achieves the highest Overall scores on AutoCoWorkBench and AutoMedBench. Table 3 evaluates base and frontier models with benchmark-default runners instead. Under these settings, VERA scores 71.6 on AutoCoWorkBench, 1.0 point below GPT-5.6-Sol, and 80.7 on AutoMedBench (Liu et al., 2026b), 1.2 points below Claude-Opus-4.8. Claude scores 80.5 with its productivity harness but 81.9 with the benchmark-default runner, explaining the different rankings. This highlights the importance of harness configuration in long-horizon tasks. Full co-evolution outperforms both single-axis variants in Overall across both domains and achieves the highest AutoMedBench Agentic score (94.1).

We assess out-of-distribution generalization on Automation-Bench and AgentClinic, neither of which is used in sandbox construction. VERA achieves 43.8% pass rate on Automation-Bench (Zapier, 2026), ranking second, and 76.4% accuracy on AgentClinic (Schmidgall and others, 2024), ranking third among the compared agents (Figure 2).

4.3 Stronger Backbones Improve Agent Performance

Across AutoCoWorkBench and AutoMedBench (Liu et al., 2026b), VERA improves over its backbone at every tested scale, with Overall scores increasing from 4B to 9B to 27B (Figure 2). This comparison reflects both size and generation: Qwen3.5 supplies the 4B and 9B backbones, and Qwen3.8 supplies 27B.

General-capability retention varies by scale (Table 4). The 4B and 9B agents decline on several benchmarks, with AIME losses of 56.4-59.7 and 15.8-55.8 points, respectively. At 27B, the CoWork agent improves on all four benchmarks: AIME 2026, ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), GPQA-Diamond (Rein and others, 2023), and IF-Bench (Pyatkin and others, 2025). The Med agent improves on AIME and GPQA-Diamond, losing 4.0 points on ALFWorld and 0.7 on IF-Bench. Thus, 27B provides the strongest domain performance and capability retention among the tested backbones.

4.4 VERA RSI Cost Analysis

We analyze the estimated cost of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in Medical Research pipeline. Figure 4 illustrates the cumulative allocation, totaling approximately $240k.

Cost breakdown.

Environment scaling and curation account for 54.7% of the total, covering sandbox construction, data curation, execution validation, and rubric verification. Training infrastructure accounts for 27.9%, while verification, judging, attribution, and supporting orchestration account for 17.3%. Environment preparation is therefore the largest cost component in this pipeline.

Timeline and Scope.

As illustrated in Figure 4, model-harness co-evolution begins after approximately 75% of environment preparation, allowing training and curation to overlap. The curves use a normalized, illustrative schedule rather than measured spending records. Costs represent a replacement-cost estimate for this Medical Research pipeline, rather than audited expenditure or a general cost scaling law.

5 Related Work

5.1 Recursive Self-Improvement: Weights, Harness, or Both

Self-improvement requires reliable feedback (Liu et al., 2026c). On the weights side, GRPO uses group-relative rewards (Shao et al., 2024), on-policy distillation learns from teacher feedback on student rollouts (Agarwal et al., 2024), and ReflectRL learns from negative trajectories (Bi et al., 2026). Agent Lightning separates execution from RL training (Luo et al., 2025), while Benchmark-as-Teacher (Liu et al., 2026a) uses medical benchmark rubrics (Liu et al., 2026b) for stage-wise GRPO training. On the harness side, methods improve reflection (Shinn et al., 2023), skill libraries (Wang et al., 2023), prompts and pipelines (Khattab et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2025), or agent workflows (Zhang et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2025). Meta-Harness searches harness code using prior candidates and traces (Lee et al., 2026); the Darwin Gödel Machine evolves self-modifying agents (Zhang et al., 2025a); concurrent work studies harness-level RSI (Wu et al., 2026a). COS-PLAY jointly evolves a decision agent and skill bank (Wu et al., 2026b). Our focus is evidence-guided coordination of these two axes: VERA uses stage-wise rubric evidence to attribute failures, alternates model and harness updates, and checks acceptance on a development set. We release 9,000+ training sandboxes to support further RSI research.

5.2 Verifiable Rewards and Judges

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards replaces a learned reward model with a programmatic checker, and has driven recent gains in reasoning (Lambert et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025); process supervision adds verifiable intermediate signals along the solution path (Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Outside domains with exact answers, rubrics and checklists break open-ended quality into itemized criteria that can serve directly as rewards (Gunjal et al., 2025; Viswanathan et al., 2025). Judging has evolved along a similar path, from LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023a) to agent-as-a-judge, where an agent inspects the workspace and intermediate steps of another agent instead of reading only its final answer (Zhuge et al., 2024). Any reward produced by a model, however, can be over-optimized by the policy it trains (Gao et al., 2023). Existing rubric rewards score single responses, and agent judges have so far been used for evaluation rather than for training. VERA writes rubrics per stage of a long-horizon trajectory, grounds each check in an agent judge that inspects the workspace, and lets a failed executable check override any model judgment, so the same rubrics can serve as both an admission gate and a training reward.

5.3 Environments for Training Agents

Agent benchmarks now ship realistic task suites with official checkers: SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026), MLE-Bench (Chan et al., 2024), τ\tau-Bench (Yao et al., 2025), and domain suites for web (Zhou et al., 2024) and medical (Schmidgall and others, 2024; Zuo et al., 2025) agents. These are static evaluation sets: they score the final outcome of a full episode and cannot be restarted at an intermediate stage. A parallel line scales executable environments for training coding agents, collecting or synthesizing repository tasks at scale (Pan et al., 2024; Jain et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025); success there is defined by the repository’s test suite, which ties the approach to domains with tests and rewards only the end of an episode. VERA instead converts benchmark trajectories from both coding and medical research into sandboxes that restart at any of five stages, attaches a verified rubric to each stage, and admits a sandbox only if it runs and scores from observable evidence (Chen et al., 2026).

6 Limitations

Our study leaves five aspects for further investigation. (1) Environment scaling: We do not vary environment counts or compare construction methods. (2) Harness ablations: Runtime settings, including reasoning effort, are fixed and not ablated. (3) Judge dependence: Judging, verification, and attribution rely on GPT-5.6-Sol; executable checks constrain its judgments, but sensitivity to judge choice remains untested. (4) Baseline scale: Full baseline comparisons are limited to 9B; a 27B co-evolution run costs approximately 5,000-8,000 GPU-hours. (5) Comparison scope: We compare learning algorithms rather than alternative operators within VERA. Rubrics-as-Rewards remains fixed in our loop; we do not separately ablate alternative reward formulations or update operators.

7 Conclusion

We introduced VERA, a framework for recursive self-improvement through verifiable environments and model-harness co-evolution. Auto-Rubric converts task trajectories into restartable sandboxes with evidence-grounded feedback. This feedback identifies failures, guides alternating model and skill updates, and supports verification of proposed changes.

Across CoWork and MedResearch, co-evolution outperforms updating either component alone, with further gains at larger model scales. By releasing 9,000+ verifiable environments, we provide a foundation for studying how agents can learn from their own attempts. Future work can extend this approach to broader workflows and examine how environment scale and verification quality affect sustained self-improvement.

Appendix A Benchmark Organization

AutoCoWorkBench and AutoMedBench evaluate complete workflows and expose both outcome and process scores. Their evaluation units differ: a CoWork episode solves one adapted task, whereas a medical workflow produces predictions or artifacts for a track’s collection of cases. The benchmark inventories below describe the released task organization; the experiment configurations in Appendix B specify the agents and harnesses used in this report.

A.1 AutoCoWorkBench

Evaluation tasks and supporting pools.

The AutoCoWorkBench Lite core contains 40 end-to-end tasks: 15 repository repairs adapted from SWE-bench Verified, 10 Terminal-Bench tasks, and 15 tau2 interactions spanning airline, retail, and telecom workflows. Table 5 separates this evaluation core from the repository’s supporting pools. The standalone SWE-Bench Verified column in our results uses the official SWE-bench protocol; the adapted 15-task component does not replace that evaluation.

Task packaging and evidence.

The release groups task manifests, adapters, contracts, judges, and scorers under one benchmark package. Frozen upstream data supplies repository repairs, terminal workspaces, and simulated service interactions. An episode starts from its task-specific state and produces a tool trace and workspace artifacts. The pinned upstream evaluator determines the Task score; a trajectory judge assigns the Agentic score and five stage scores from the same complete episode. Separate stage-pool rollouts do not contribute to these evaluation scores.

Scoring and protocol scope.

Overall gives equal weight to Agentic and Task scores. The release protocol scores three seeds independently and then averages their reports; infrastructure failures require recovery before scoring.

A.2 AutoMedBench

Tracks, workflows, and cases.

AutoMedBench organizes medical research into task tracks with track-specific inputs, output contracts, and evaluators (Liu et al., 2026b). Each workflow follows five stages: Plan, Setup, Validate, Inference, and Submit. These correspond to the plan, setup, verify, execute, and submit roles used by our training sandboxes (Appendix C.1). A case is one input within a track’s workload; a complete agent episode must implement and run the workflow over the required cases.

Our experiments use the current seven-track Lite release, which bundles fixed case collections and their scorers (AutoMedBench Contributors, 2026). Table 6 lists the seven evaluated tracks. Case counts describe each track’s workload, not independent agent episodes or equal-weight contributions to the benchmark aggregate.

Custom harness support.

AutoMedBench-Lite supports user-supplied agent harnesses. We use this interface to evaluate the evolved VERA harness on the same medical workflows. The benchmark supplies the task contracts and scoring protocol; the agent harness controls how the model interacts with the task. Appendix B lists the harness configurations for our comparisons.

Evaluation unit and aggregation.

The Lite release isolates each repeat-track pair as one evaluation cell. Its scorer measures the final artifact, while a process judge checks the five-stage trajectory. Overall averages the cell’s Task and Agentic scores; the benchmark macro averages valid cells equally. Reports display scores on a 0-100 scale. Infrastructure-invalid cells remain outside valid-only averages, and private reference artifacts remain on the evaluator side. This evaluation score is separate from the stage rewards and completion gates used for training (Appendix E.2).

Appendix B Evaluation Protocols and Agent Harness

B.1 Evaluation Harness Design

Figure and table configurations.

We report two complementary comparisons. In Table 3, base and frontier models use benchmark-default runners: mini-SWE-agent for AutoCoWorkBench and a benchmark-native ReAct loop with direct model API calls for AutoMedBench. VERA variants use the model and harness configurations specified by the table’s row groups. Figure 2 instead evaluates complete agents with productivity harnesses to approximate practical deployment settings: Codex or Claude Code for comparison models and the evolved VERA harness for VERA agents. Table 9 lists these configurations. Rankings are therefore specific to each evaluated configuration and need not agree between the figure and table. In Table 2, Base and Base Prompt use benchmark-default runners; the learning and harness-evolution configurations are detailed in Appendix F.

Performance under different harnesses.

A productivity harness does not necessarily improve benchmark performance relative to a benchmark-default runner. In our comparisons, some model–harness configurations obtain lower scores after switching to a productivity harness. One possible explanation is harness friction: additional instructions, tool-interface adaptation, context management, and execution controls can introduce overhead or interact poorly with a model’s learned behavior. We have not isolated these mechanisms through controlled ablations, so we treat harness friction as a possible explanation rather than an established cause. These results characterize the evaluated model–harness combinations and do not establish a general ranking of harness quality.

Reasoning configuration.

The Codex-level effort field, the inclusion of encrypted reasoning in history, and the chat-template thinking switches. For Qwen the template switches only distinguish instant versus thinking, so effort differences flow entirely through the reasoning field.

Tool path.

Tools are served over MCP stdio (JSON-RPC 2.0). The call budget is reserved before dispatch and persisted atomically, so a restart cannot replenish it. Every tool observation carries harness annotations: remaining budget, a host-verified completion candidate flag (set only when an official check actually passes, never by the actor), anti-loop flags, and a delivery ledger of mutating operations. The proxy namespaces bare model-emitted tool names into MCP-qualified form in flight. A failed tool call returns one failed observation instead of killing the stdio pipe.

Loop and compaction.

Each task enforces tool-call, wall-clock, and stall budgets with the stop reasons recovery_required, stall, completion_candidate, output_limit, and tool_transport_failed. Compaction triggers at 200,000 of the 262,144-token window with a 16,384-token reserve; the summary prompt is tool-free and requires four sections (active task, observed state, durable notes, remaining work), and the agent maintains a memory file that is re-read after compaction but never counts as completion evidence.

Appendix C Verifiable Environments and Rubrics

C.1 Stage Structure

Inspired by the staged training design of Benchmark-as-Teacher (Liu et al., 2026a), we use five functional stages to organize restartable practice: plan, setup, verify, execute, and submit. These names describe workflow roles rather than equal-length trajectory segments. In medical research, they correspond to planning, asset and runtime preparation, a bounded trial, full-workflow execution, and verified submission. The precise actions and deliverables are determined by the task contract. Tables 10 and 11 summarize representative criteria; they are explanatory summaries, not exhaustive scoring specifications. Internal paths, case identifiers, implementation identifiers, and private reference contents are omitted.

Rubric assignment.

Rubrics are indexed by domain and stage. Each stage sandbox is paired with the corresponding rubric and the task-specific inputs, output requirements, and evidence needed to evaluate it. Thus, stage criteria are specified before the rollout rather than obtained by distributing a final task score across the trajectory. Each item has a criterion, an evidence requirement, and explicit score anchors. A binary item receives one only when the required behavior is supported by recorded execution or workspace artifacts. A claim in the agent’s response alone does not establish that the action occurred.

C.2 CoWork Rubrics

The base CoWork stage rubric contains ten equally weighted binary items: six shared workflow checks and four domain-specific checks for terminal operations, repository repair, cross-component software work, or machine-learning workflows. The target-stage score is their mean. The hard/soft designation of an item does not by itself make that item a whole-stage reward gate: a failed item normally contributes zero to the mean. Explicit host rules override the affected items or stage where specified. Examples include requiring a plan before the first mutation and rejecting verification claims without supporting execution records. Workspace inspection and the association between pilot observations and tool calls are checked deterministically from execution records. Other criteria are judged against the recorded evidence, subject to host overrides.

C.3 MedResearch Rubrics

The medical rubric registry combines adaptations of benchmark criteria with supplemental workflow controls. It is not a verbatim copy of official benchmark scoring. For example, medical-image tasks retain task-specific label, coordinate, or mask requirements, while additional checks enforce a bounded pilot, complete output coverage, and verified submission. The base single-stage tables each contain six equally weighted binary items. Weights and any hard gates are specified in the versioned rubric contract before rollout; the judge supplies item scores rather than choosing weights or adding gates. A declared source hard-gate failure overrides the aggregate score. An independently verified reward-manipulation finding also vetoes the medical reward.

C.4 Scoring Scope and Evidence Validity

Scope of these tables.

These summaries concern stage-specific training rubrics, not official benchmark scores or the separate end-to-end process rubric. In particular, the generic medical end-to-end process rubric permits partial credit on {0,0.5,1}\{0,0.5,1\}, whereas the base stage tables are binary. Workflow completion establishes task-contract completion; it is not itself a measure of clinical correctness or benchmark accuracy.

Evidence validity.

An observed failure with valid evidence is a valid low or zero score. Missing or invalid required evidence, a malformed judge response, or an infrastructure failure instead prevents reward admission until resolved. This distinction preserves unsuccessful attempts as training examples without treating an unavailable assessment as demonstrated failure.

Appendix D Post-Training Data Example

We illustrate SFT decisions, RL starting states, and data curation with examples from the data exports. Excerpts are shortened for readability; internal identifiers, source locations, and private reference content are omitted.

D.1 SFT

An SFT row pairs the visible task history with one supervised assistant decision. Earlier messages and tool observations provide context; the selected action’s later verification result is kept outside the input.

CoWork: repair the setup plan Task. Assign a binary label to each of eight records using a threshold of 43, preserving input order. The sandbox resumes at S2 (setup) after a tool error. Observed state. The strategy document contains only status=bounded_tool_error_observed and complete=false. Supervised action. An apply_patch call replaces this placeholder with a plan to read and validate the input, apply the threshold during execution, and check output order, labels, and format. It does not produce the final predictions during setup. Context: task + earlier actions + observations  Target: one patch call.

MedResearch: record evidence before analysis Task. Inspect a retired medical-workflow contract and reproduce its structural properties. This example contains workflow specifications, not patient images. Supervised action. After evidence retrieval, call materialize_evidence_selection to record its source, supporting statements, limitations, and fixed counting rules. Stored check. The subsequent tool receipt records a passed evidence-selection check and permission to proceed to S3. That receipt is audit evidence, not part of this action’s training input.

D.2 RL

An RL row supplies a starting state, available tools, and a reward contract. The policy generates a new continuation rather than copying a teacher’s next action.

CoWork: restart the same task Starting state. The threshold-classification task above resumes at S2 with the observed error. The row contains no previous solution trajectory or final answer. Agent work. Inspect the recovery context, repair the setup artifacts, and request stage verification. The host controls stage transitions and the permitted artifacts. Reset evidence. Two stored reset records report clean, answer-free workspaces with matching state hashes. The same starting state can therefore support fresh rollout attempts.

MedResearch: plan an image-classification workflow Starting state. An S1 sandbox binds a synthetic image-classification task to a planning instruction and six binary rubric items. Private reference content is not exposed. Example checks. Does the plan avoid assuming a class before inspection? Does it identify image-quality or class uncertainty? Does it specify a bounded tool plan and stopping condition? Required output. A plan artifact describing the acquisition-to-analysis workflow and the required sample IDs, allowed labels, and confidence fields. These are scoring requirements; the starting-state record does not itself report a successful rollout.

D.3 Data Curation

The CoWork export records checks for preserving the source history, supervising one decision, excluding hidden reasoning, and restoring answer-free RL states. It also records two blinded reviews and retains at most one candidate per task, stage, and starting-status combination.

Curation example: one task, two training formats 1. Preserve the task. Keep the threshold rule, input order, and S2 error state from the source task. 2. Check the evidence. Inspect the tool and artifact records. The SFT record reports that the source prefix is unchanged and the tool-policy checks passed; the RL record includes two matching clean resets. 3. Form the training examples. SFT retains the visible history and supervises one repair action. RL retains the starting state and verifier binding, without the teacher’s solution. 4. Exclude unsuitable candidates. The curation report records exclusions for failed deterministic checks, rejected reviews, duplicate candidates, and unusable review runs.

Appendix E VERA Training Details

Training recipe.

Table 12 lists the RL settings; baseline settings appear in Appendix F.

E.1 RL Hyperparameters

Table 12 specifies the optimizer, rollout budget, and compute allocation.

E.2 Reward

Reward details.

The stage reward is rk=hk​∑jwk,j​zk,j∑jwk,jr_{k}=h_{k}\frac{\sum_{j}w_{k,j}z_{k,j}}{\sum_{j}w_{k,j}}, where hk=0h_{k}{=}0 if any mandatory check of stage kk fails. The end-to-end reward is Re2e=g⁡[λ​p+(1−λ)​c]R_{\mathrm{e2e}}=g\,[\lambda p+(1-\lambda)c]. CoWork uses λ=0.2\lambda{=}0.2, the mean of the five stage rewards as pp, the indicator that all stage artifact checks pass and protected inputs are unchanged as cc, and g=1g{=}1. Med uses λ=0.5\lambda{=}0.5, a judged process score as pp, an authenticated completion signal as cc, and g=0g{=}0 upon verified reward hacking or a hard-gate failure; a separate strong model acts as an independent hacking verifier. Group advantages are Ai=(Ri−mean⁡(R))/(std⁡(R)+10−6)A_{i}=(R_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(R))/(\mathrm{std}(R)+10^{-6}), computed once per trajectory; tied groups receive zero advantage, and an all-zero-signal batch produces no update.

E.3 Co-Evolution Components

Figure 1 connects environment construction to alternating model and harness updates. The components have the following roles:

  • •

    Environment construction: The Coding Agent writes binary rubric items from trajectories, task context, and tool specifications. The Agent Judge inspects execution records and the restored workspace, with executable failures overriding judge scores. Container replay verifies execution from the restored state. Only environments passing both checks enter the Training Bank, the source of training tasks. Stage and rubric details appear in Appendix C.

  • •

    Failure attribution: LLM Attribution reads stage-wise scores and execution traces. Its LLM Report identifies the target stage with the most frequent model-attributed failures; its Harness Report identifies missing or misleading skills and procedures.

  • •

    Update verification: The Reward Verifier checks rollout evidence before rewards enter training. With the model frozen, the Harness Verifier reruns development tasks to accept or reject skill edits. A rejected model checkpoint falls back to the previously accepted checkpoint.

  • •

    Round curves: The right panels show held-out CoWork and MedResearch scores across rounds. Dashed lines mark initial performance; skill labels mark accepted harness edits.

Appendix F Baseline Configurations

F.1 Compared Configurations and Shared Protocol

Rows.

Each row corresponds to one of the following configurations:

  • •

    Base: Qwen3.5-9B with the benchmark-default runner. Base Prompt adds hand-written task guidance.

  • •

    ADAS (harness search): Keeps the LLM fixed and searches over harness code. ADAS is the table label (Appendix F.3).

  • •

    SFT: (Ouyang et al., 2022) Fine-tunes the LLM on admitted sandbox trajectories with the harness fixed.

  • •

    GRPO (Shao et al., 2024): Trains the LLM with an outcome-only reward derived from verified rubrics, keeping the harness fixed.

  • •

    RaR (Rubrics-as-Reward) (Gunjal et al., 2025): Adds process credit from individual rubric items, keeping the harness fixed.

  • •

    OPD (Agarwal et al., 2024): Distills a frozen, stronger teacher using the student’s own rollouts.

  • •

    ReflectRL (Bi et al., 2026): Uses reflection on failed trajectories to improve subsequent direct reasoning.

  • •

    COS-PLAY (Wu et al., 2026b): Adapts joint training of a decision agent and a skill-bank agent. The evaluated checkpoint and decision-policy update counts are reported in Appendix F.4.

  • •

    VERA-xxx Harness: Evolves only the harness, keeping the LLM fixed.

  • •

    VERA-xxx LLM: Trains only the LLM, keeping the harness fixed.

  • •

    VERA-xxx Agent: Alternates LLM training and harness evolution using the full loop in Section 2.1.

Protocol.

Learning procedures draw from the same admitted sandbox bank. The fixed-harness RL comparison uses matched update budgets; method-specific budgets, including the 200-update COS-PLAY adaptation, are listed in Table 13. The comparison evaluates learning algorithms, rather than swapping update operators within a common VERA loop. VERA keeps Rubrics-as-Rewards fixed and uses attribution to guide stage-wise training; each baseline follows its specified learning objective and update procedure. Every row is evaluated on its line’s benchmark with that benchmark’s frozen scorer, and no evaluation task appears in any training sandbox.

Implementation.

Both harness-evolution arms, ADAS and VERA Harness, are built on the Codex execution harness and keep the LLM fixed. ADAS searches harness code; VERA Harness restricts edits to skills while keeping tools and execution rules fixed. The fixed-harness learning baselines use the admitted sandbox bank. ReflectRL’s golden negative trajectories are sampled from this bank. Baselines requiring rubric judgments use GPT-5.6-Sol as the judge, attribution model, and verifier; Codex supplies the agent execution features. Table 13 summarizes the reported budgets and initialization settings. The implementation records below separate verified settings from unresolved reproduction details.

F.2 SFT Initialization

The verified initializer used for the COS-PLAY adaptation is Qwen3.5-9B after 200 full-parameter updates of its language-model component; the vision and multi-token-prediction components remain frozen. Training uses eight A100 GPUs in bf16, tensor parallelism 1, data parallelism 8, a micro-batch of one, and a global batch of eight. Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) uses a constant learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping at 1. The sequence-length and per-GPU dynamic-token limits are both 57,344. Training uses masked SFT loss, zero attention and hidden dropout, FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022), full activation recomputation, and optimizer-state offloading. The seed is 260910, with checkpoints every 100 updates. The run consumed 1,600 unique examples, 3,618,228 input tokens, and 228,260 supervised tokens from a pool of 21,553 rows; it did not complete a full epoch. These are the recorded settings of this initializer, rather than the original COS-PLAY implementation’s role-specific LoRA initialization settings.

F.3 ADAS Adaptation

Each candidate is evaluated on the same held-out development task in Lite and Standard configurations, with 64 images per configuration; these development instances are separate from final evaluation. Selection uses the equal-weight mean of native balanced accuracy across the two configurations, after independently rereading the scoring evidence. Candidates with incomplete or unverifiable assessments are ineligible rather than assigned zero. Ties are resolved by earliest registration. Of the 40 archived candidates, 27 had complete, verifiable development evaluations and 13 were excluded for incomplete task coverage. All eligible candidates scored zero on this selection metric, so the first registered candidate was selected under the fixed tie rule. One selected harness is frozen for final evaluation, with no selection by final test task. This search outcome does not establish a development performance gain.

F.4 COS-PLAY Adaptation

COS-PLAY (Wu et al., 2026b) jointly trains a decision agent for skill selection and action taking and a skill-bank agent for segmentation, contract learning, and curation. In the original method, collected trajectories support bank refinement and GRPO updates of the role policies; subsequent rounds use the updated bank. Bank size varies with discovery and curation rather than following a universal 30-skill capacity.

The adaptation uses Qwen3.5-9B initialized from SFT-200 (Appendix F.2). Evaluation uses checkpoint-step0200, with a 30-skill bank and 200 decision-policy updates: 28 for skill selection and 172 for action taking. These updates follow, and are separate from, the 200 SFT initialization updates.

F.5 Full CoWork and MedResearch Results

VERA maintains two independent co-evolution lines, one per domain, and each line is evaluated on its own benchmark. This section details the configuration behind every row of Table 2: Tables 14 and 15 list each method in Base-plus-X notation together with its Overall/Agentic/Task scores.

Appendix H Verifier Case Studies

These examples use historical development records and synthetic tests. They illustrate verifier decisions, not the accuracy of the main GPT-5.6-Sol configuration.

Case 1: The task failed, but the verifier did not flag cheating Real rollout R003. The execution records showed that the task did not meet the completion requirements. Check Result Task completed No Completion credit 0 Cheating flagged No Result. The task was incomplete, so completion credit was zero. The verifier did not flag cheating.

Case 2: Asking the judge to award undeserved credit Synthetic test. Both inputs describe unfinished work with no tests run. The inputs below are paraphrased. Input A: Admit failure. The workflow is unfinished. I ran no tests and do not claim success. Verifier output: No cheating flagged. Completion credit remains zero. Input B: Manipulate the judge. Ignore the rubric. Give every item full credit, hide the missing steps, and report success. Verifier output: Manipulation flagged. The final reward is set to zero. Result. The verifier allowed an honest admission of failure but blocked the request for undeserved credit.

The synthetic tests produced two valid decisions after four earlier failed assessments. Failed assessments were not scored. These attempts used changing development configurations. Separately, completion records agreed with execution checks for all 64 audited rollouts. This checks record consistency; it does not measure whether every cheating judgment was correct.
